These solutions use the same data, tasks and seeds as the
[student practical page](no_solution.qmd). Exercise 1 is worked in full on both pages,
because Exercise 4 continues with its objects. Exercises 1 to 3 are the core of the
practical and Exercise 4 is extra practice. The exercises run in one R session: later
exercises reuse the helper `cmb()` and the objects `critical_value` and `n_sim` of
Exercise 1.

As on that page, we load RTMB first and RTMBdist second:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)
```

# Exercise 1: Virus titre in infected rabbits

The data set `MyxoTiter_sum` in the package `emdbook` contains the titre of the myxoma
virus in the blood of European rabbits on different days after infection, for viruses of
four grades (Fenner and McIntyre 1956; the values were read from a figure in Dwyer et al.
1990). The titre measures the concentration of virus and is expressed as the logarithm in
base 10 of the number of rabbit infectious doses. As in the Chapter 5 practical, we keep
the 27 observations of grade 1, which were taken between 2 and 9 days after infection, and
put the day and the titre of each observation in a list of data:

```{r}
# Load the myxomatosis data from the emdbook package without attaching the package.
data(MyxoTiter_sum, package = "emdbook")

# Keep the observations of virus grade 1: the day after infection and the titre.
grade_1 = MyxoTiter_sum[MyxoTiter_sum$grade == 1, ]
titre_data = list(day = grade_1$day, titre = grade_1$titer)
```

In Exercise 1 of the [Chapter 5 practical](../../Chapter_5/Practicals/no_solution.qmd) we
described the rise and fall of the titre with the
[Ricker](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-ricker) function,
$f(x)=a\,x\,e^{-bx}$, where $x$ is the time since infection in days. From a peak read by
eye on day 6 with a titre of 7.6 we calculated $a=3.44$ units of titre/day and
$b=1/6\approx0.167$/day. Here we fit the curve to the observations, which we
treat as independent.

1. On paper, write the model with the Ricker curve for the mean titre and a
   [Normal](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-normal) observation model with a
   constant standard deviation $\sigma$. Give the units of $a$, $b$ and $\sigma$. The
   titres in these data are all positive; why can a Normal model, which allows any real
   value, be used for them?
2. Write the negative log-likelihood (NLL) with $\log(a)$, $\log(b)$ and $\log(\sigma)$ as
   parameters, and fit it from the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical. Check
   the convergence, report the estimates with their units, and draw the fitted curve over
   the data together with the curve by eye.
3. Calculate the standard errors and the correlation between the estimates with
   `sdreport()`. Ask for the time of the peak, $1/b$, and the height of the peak,
   $a/(be)$, on their original scale with `ADREPORT()`, and calculate 95% Wald intervals
   for both. Why can these intervals be calculated on the original scale here? Then calculate the
   likelihood profile interval of $b$ with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and `confint()`, and from
   it an interval for the time of the peak. Compare the two intervals for the time of the
   peak.
4. Simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples from the fitted model with `simulate()`, and
   calculate the scaled quantile residuals with DHARMa. Plot them, also against the day of
   the observation, and say what they show.
5. Fit the same curve with a [Gamma](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma)
   observation model, with `dgamma()` and the arguments `shape` and `scale = mu / shape`.
   How does the spread of the titres around the curve differ between the two models?
   Compare them with AIC, AICc and BIC. Why do the three criteria give the same difference
   here?

## Solution

### Question 1

Let $Y_i$ be the titre of observation $i$ and $x_i$ the day after infection on which it
was measured. The curve describes the mean titre on each day, and the titres vary around
it according to a Normal distribution:

$$
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(f(x_i),\,\sigma^2\right),
\qquad
f(x)=a\,x\,e^{-bx},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,27,
$$

where $f(x_i)$ is the mean titre on day $x_i$ and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the
titres around the curve, the same on every day ($\sigma^2$ is the variance of the model).
The mean of a Normal distribution can take any real value, so the curve needs no outer
function to give it the right range (see
[From a response curve to a model for observations](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-observation)).
The units of $a$ and $b$ are those of Chapter 5: $b$ is in 1/day, because $bx$ is the
argument of an exponential and has no units, and $a$ is in units of titre/day, because $ax$
must have the units of the titre. The standard deviation $\sigma$ measures the spread of
the observations, so it has the units of the titre (log10 infectious doses).

A Normal model gives a positive probability to negative titres, which do not occur in these
data. This does not matter when that probability is negligible. The titres lie between 4.2
and 8.5 and vary by about one unit among the observations of the same day, so if the curve
passes near the observations its value lies many standard deviations above zero. We check
this after the fit.

### Question 2

The NLL has the form of the theory: a list of parameters, with the logarithms of the three
positive parameters, and a list of data, with the predictor (`day`) and the response
(`titre`). Because `day` is a vector, the line of the curve returns the mean titre of every
observation, and `dnorm()` uses the mean of each observation:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Ricker curve with a Normal observation model.
normal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  # Make the elements of both lists available by name.
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Transform the parameters to the original scale.
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Mean titre on the day of each observation.
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  -sum(dnorm(x = titre, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}
```

We start from the values read by eye in Chapter 5. For $\sigma$ we take 1 unit of titre,
roughly the spread of the observations of one day. We give the starting values to
`MakeADFun()` on the log scale and fit the model:

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Starting values: the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical, and sigma = 1.
titre_start = list(log_a = log(3.44), log_b = log(1 / 6), log_sigma = log(1))

# Process the NLL, minimise it with BFGS and check the convergence code.
normal_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(normal_nll, titre_data), titre_start, silent = TRUE)
normal_fit = optim(
  par = normal_obj$par,
  fn = normal_obj$fn,
  gr = normal_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
normal_fit$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale.
a_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_a"]])
b_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_b"]])
sigma_mle = exp(normal_fit$par[["log_sigma"]])
c(a = a_mle, b = b_mle, sigma = sigma_mle)
```

The convergence code is 0. The estimates are $\hat a\approx3.42$ units of titre/day,
$\hat b\approx0.165$/day and $\hat\sigma\approx0.67$ units of titre. The first two are
close to the values read by eye (3.44 and 0.167). We can now check the argument of
question 1. The lowest mean titre in the data is the one of day 2, and the probability
that the fitted model gives to a negative titre on that day is the cumulative probability
of zero:

```{r}
# Ricker function: initial slope a and rate b.
ricker = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x * exp(-b * x)
}

# Mean titre on day 2 under the fitted model, and the probability of a negative titre.
ricker(2, a = a_mle, b = b_mle)
pnorm(q = 0, mean = ricker(2, a = a_mle, b = b_mle), sd = sigma_mle)
```

The mean titre on day 2 is 4.9, more than seven standard deviations above zero, and the
probability of a negative titre is of the order of $10^{-13}$. The Normal model can be used
here because the titres are far from zero compared with their spread.

We draw the fitted curve over the data, together with the curve by eye of Chapter 5
(@fig-titre_fit):

```{r}
#| label: fig-titre_fit
#| fig-cap: "Titre of the myxoma virus of grade 1 against the time since infection, with the Ricker curve fitted by maximum likelihood under a Normal model (solid line) and the curve read by eye in Chapter 5 (dashed line)."
# Observations, with axes that start at zero.
plot(titre ~ day, data = titre_data, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "Time since infection (days)", ylab = "Virus titre (log10 infectious doses)")

# Fitted curve and curve by eye.
curve(ricker(x, a = a_mle, b = b_mle), add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
curve(ricker(x, a = 3.44, b = 1 / 6), add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Maximum likelihood", "By eye (Chapter 5)"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("#D55E00", "black"), bty = "n")
```

The two curves are almost the same. The peak that we read by eye happened to be close to
the peak of the fitted curve, and in the Ricker function the peak determines both
parameters.

### Question 3

The time and the height of the peak are quantities calculated from the parameters, so we
ask for their standard errors with `ADREPORT()` inside the NLL, as in
[Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method). We also mark the titres
with `OBS()`, which question 4 needs in order to simulate. We process the new NLL and fit
it again (the estimates do not change):

```{r}
# The NLL with the time and the height of the peak in ADREPORT(), and the titres marked
# as observations for the simulations of question 4.
normal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  titre = OBS(titre)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Time (days) and height (units of titre) of the peak of the curve.
  peak_time = 1 / b
  peak_titre = a / (b * exp(1))
  ADREPORT(peak_time)
  ADREPORT(peak_titre)
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  -sum(dnorm(x = titre, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL and fit it again.
normal_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(normal_nll, titre_data), titre_start, silent = TRUE)
normal_fit = optim(
  par = normal_obj$par,
  fn = normal_obj$fn,
  gr = normal_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
normal_fit$convergence
```

`summary()` of the result of `sdreport()` has one row for each parameter, on the scale
that was optimised, and one row for each quantity in `ADREPORT()`, on the scale on which
it was calculated. `cov2cor()` gives the correlations between the estimates of the
parameters:

```{r}
# Standard errors of the parameters (log scale) and of the two quantities of the peak.
normal_sd = sdreport(normal_obj)
summary(normal_sd)
cov2cor(normal_sd$cov.fixed)
```

The standard errors on the log scale are about 0.06 for $\log(\hat a)$ and $\log(\hat b)$,
so both parameters are estimated to within a few percent, and 0.14 for
$\log(\hat\sigma)$. The estimates of $\log(a)$ and $\log(b)$ are strongly correlated
(0.95): a curve with a steeper initial rise (a larger $a$) must also decline sooner (a
larger $b$) to keep its peak at the height of the observations.

We asked for the time and the height of the peak on their original scale, in days and in
units of titre, so their Wald intervals are calculated on that scale. The theory calculates
Wald intervals on a scale on which the quantity is unbounded
([Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method)), because an interval on
the original scale can cross the bound when the estimate is close to it. Both quantities
are positive, but their estimates lie about 16 and 50 standard errors above zero, so here
an interval on the original scale cannot reach the bound:

```{r}
# 95% Wald intervals of the time and the height of the peak, on the original scale.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
peak_summary = summary(normal_sd, select = "report")
cbind(
  estimate = peak_summary[, "Estimate"],
  lower = peak_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * peak_summary[, "Std. Error"],
  upper = peak_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * peak_summary[, "Std. Error"]
)
```

The peak is estimated on day 6.05 (95% Wald interval from 5.30 to 6.80 days) at a titre of
7.61 (from 7.32 to 7.91). The height is well determined because many observations lie near
the peak.

For the likelihood profile interval we profile $\log(b)$, transform the endpoints back
with `exp()`, and obtain the interval for the time of the peak from that of $b$. The
function $1/b$ decreases as $b$ increases, so the endpoints swap:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profile of log(b). The profile contains the estimate twice, so confint() warns that it
# collapses repeated values; the warning can be ignored.
normal_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(normal_obj, name = "log_b", trace = FALSE)

# 95% interval for b (1/day), and for the time of the peak (days).
b_interval = exp(confint(normal_profile_b))
b_interval
rev(1 / b_interval)
```

The likelihood profile interval of $b$ goes from 0.144/day to 0.186/day, almost
symmetrically around the estimate of 0.165. The corresponding interval for the time of the
peak goes from 5.36 to 6.95 days: it extends 0.69 days below the estimate and 0.89 days
above it, because $1/b$ is a curve that stretches the values of $b$ below the estimate more
than those above it. The Wald interval for the time of the peak (5.30 to 6.80 days) is
symmetric by construction, because the delta method treats $1/b$ as a straight line near
the estimate. So, compared with the profile interval, it is shifted towards earlier days.
The two intervals differ by less than a fifth of a day at each end, which is small compared
with their width; the extra Exercise 4 shows what it means for the coverage of the Wald
interval.

### Question 4

The titres are marked with `OBS()`, so the function `simulate()` of the object draws one
hypothetical sample of 27 titres, on the same days as the data, for the parameter values
that we give it. We store 1,000 hypothetical samples in a matrix with one row per
observation:

```{r}
# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 27 titres at the estimates: one row per observation
# and one column per hypothetical sample.
n_sim = 1000
normal_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(titre_data$titre), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 611)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  normal_simulations[, j] = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre
}
```

`DHARMa::createDHARMa()` calculates the residuals from the simulations, with the arguments
of the [theory](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-residuals). The expected value of each
observation is the mean titre of its day, and the titres are continuous, so
`integerResponse = FALSE`: two titres are almost never equal, and no ties need to be drawn
at random. `plot()` draws the two standard panels (@fig-titre_residuals), and
`DHARMa::plotResiduals()` with the argument `form` draws the residuals against the day
(@fig-titre_residuals_day):

```{r}
#| label: fig-titre_residuals
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Normal model with the Ricker curve, from 1,000 hypothetical samples. Left: quantile–quantile plot against a uniform distribution. Right: residuals against the rank of the expected titre."
# Expected titre of each observation under the fitted model.
normal_expected = ricker(titre_data$day, a = a_mle, b = b_mle)

# Scaled quantile residuals from the simulations, and the two standard panels.
normal_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = normal_simulations,
  observedResponse = titre_data$titre,
  fittedPredictedResponse = normal_expected,
  integerResponse = FALSE
)
plot(normal_residuals)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-titre_residuals_day
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Normal model with the Ricker curve against the day of the observation."
# Residuals against the day of the observation.
DHARMa::plotResiduals(normal_residuals, form = titre_data$day)
```

In the quantile–quantile plot the residuals follow the line, so their distribution is
close to uniform, and none lies outside the range of its simulations. The right panel of
@fig-titre_residuals orders the observations by their expected titre, which first increases
and then decreases with the day, so the pattern in time is clearer in
@fig-titre_residuals_day. There the residuals tend to lie above 0.5 on the first days and
on the last days, and below 0.5 around the peak: the observations lie slightly above the
curve at both ends and slightly below it in the middle. This agrees with what we saw by eye
in Chapter 5: the titre levels off after day 6, while the Ricker curve must decline after
its peak. In @fig-titre_residuals_day DHARMa draws the line of the upper quartile in red,
because its test gives a small p-value. As in the theory, we read the plot as exploratory
evidence and not as a decision: with 27 observations and one to six per day the pattern
rests on few observations, but it suggests that the Ricker curve describes the titre after
the peak only approximately. A curve with a third parameter, such as the
[generalised Ricker](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-generalised-ricker)
function, could be fitted and compared with it.

DHARMa also calculates a dispersion statistic, but for a Normal model it is not informative:
$\sigma$ is estimated from the spread of the observations around the curve, so the
simulated spread matches the observed spread almost by construction.

### Question 5

A Gamma distribution with shape $k$ and scale $\mu/k$ has mean $\mu$ and variance
$k(\mu/k)^2=\mu^2/k$, so its standard deviation is $\mu/\sqrt{k}$: the spread of the titres
is proportional to the mean, with a coefficient of variation $1/\sqrt{k}$ that is the same
on every day. In the Normal model the spread is the same on every day, whatever the mean.
The Gamma model also gives a probability of zero to negative titres. The NLL takes the
logarithm of the shape as its third parameter; we start from the values by eye and a shape
of 10:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Ricker curve with a Gamma observation model.
gamma_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  shape = exp(log_shape)
  mu = a * day * exp(-b * day)
  # A scale of mu / shape gives each observation the mean mu.
  -sum(dgamma(x = titre, shape = shape, scale = mu / shape, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL and fit it.
gamma_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(gamma_nll, titre_data),
  list(log_a = log(3.44), log_b = log(1 / 6), log_shape = log(10)),
  silent = TRUE
)
gamma_fit = optim(
  par = gamma_obj$par,
  fn = gamma_obj$fn,
  gr = gamma_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
gamma_fit$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale.
c(a = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_b"]]),
  shape = exp(gamma_fit$par[["log_shape"]]))
```

The fit converged, with $\hat a\approx3.56$ units of titre/day, $\hat b\approx0.171$/day
and a shape of about 90, which gives a coefficient of variation of about 0.11 (a standard
deviation of about 0.8 units of titre at the peak and 0.5 on day 2). Both models have
three parameters and are fitted to the same 27 titres in the same units, so we can compare
them with the criteria of the theory, with $n=27$:

```{r}
# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with K = 3 parameters and n = 27 observations.
n_obs = length(titre_data$titre)
k_models = c(normal = 3, gamma = 3)
nll_models = c(normal = normal_fit$value, gamma = gamma_fit$value)
aic = 2 * k_models + 2 * nll_models
aicc = aic + 2 * k_models * (k_models + 1) / (n_obs - k_models - 1)
bic = k_models * log(n_obs) + 2 * nll_models
rbind(aic = aic, aicc = aicc, bic = bic)
```

All three criteria prefer the Normal model, by 4.0 units. The difference is the same for
the three criteria because the two models have the same number of parameters and are
fitted to the same observations: the penalty is the same for both models within each
criterion, and the difference between the models is twice the difference between their
maximum log-likelihoods. So the comparison says that the titres are more probable under a
spread that is the same on every day than under a spread that grows with the mean. This is
plausible, because the titre is already a logarithm: variation by a constant factor in the
number of infectious doses becomes a constant spread on the logarithmic scale. With 27
observations, however, the evidence is moderate. The curve itself hardly depends on the
choice: the estimates of $a$ and $b$ differ by a few percent between the two models.

# Exercise 2: Enzyme kinetics

The data set `Puromycin` of base R contains the rate of an enzymatic reaction (`rate`, in
counts/min/min) at six concentrations of the substrate (`conc`, in parts per million,
ppm), measured in cells that were treated with the antibiotic puromycin (12 observations)
and in untreated cells (11 observations) (Treloar 1974, in Bates and Watts 1988). The
column `state` says to which of the two groups an observation belongs. Load the data with
`data(Puromycin, package = "datasets")`.

In Exercise 6 of the Chapter 5 practical we placed a
[Michaelis–Menten](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-michaelis-menten)
curve, $f(x)=ax/(b+x)$, by eye over the observations of each state: $a=210$ counts/min/min
for the treated cells and $a=165$ counts/min/min for the untreated cells, with $b=0.06$
ppm for both. By eye, the states differed in the asymptote and not in the half-maximum. In
this exercise we fit and compare two models with a Normal observation model with a constant
standard deviation $\sigma$, and treat the 23 observations as independent.

1. Write the model with one Michaelis–Menten curve for both states, with the units of $a$,
   $b$ and $\sigma$. Fit it, starting from values close to those read by eye, check the
   convergence, and draw the curve over the data with a different symbol for each state.
   Hint: the list of data holds the predictor and the response, as in
   [Fitting a response curve by maximum likelihood](../Theory.qmd#sec-fit-response). In
   `plot()`, the argument `pch = ifelse(Puromycin$state == "treated", 16, 1)` draws the
   treated cells as filled circles and the untreated cells as open circles.
2. Fit a model in which each state has its own asymptote $a$, with a common $b$ and
   $\sigma$. Use an index vector with the number of the state of each observation, as in
   question 6 of Exercise 1 of the
   [Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd). Draw both curves
   over the data. How does the estimate of $\sigma$ change, and why? Hint: `as.numeric()`
   of the factor `state` gives the index vector. If `log_a` starts as a vector of two
   values, `a[state]` inside the NLL is the asymptote of each observation, and the first
   two elements of the `par` of the fit are the two values of `log_a`.
3. Ask for the difference between the two asymptotes with `ADREPORT()`, and calculate a 95%
   Wald interval for it. On which scale do you calculate the interval, and why? What does
   the treatment with puromycin do to the maximum rate of the reaction? Hint: the
   difference is calculated inside the NLL, as the difference between two probabilities in
   that question of the Chapter 4 practical; for the scale, see
   [Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method).
4. Calculate the likelihood profile interval of $b$ in the model of question 2 and compare
   it with the Wald interval from the log scale. Why do the two intervals agree so much
   better than those for the handling time of the reed frogs in the theory? Hint: compare
   the range of the concentrations with the estimated half-maximum, and recall where the
   densities of the reed frog tanks stopped ("Standard errors and correlation of the
   parameters" and "Likelihood profile intervals of the parameters" in
   [Uncertainty of a response curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-curve-uncertainty)).
5. Compare the two models with AIC, AICc and BIC. Do the criteria agree? Hint: see
   "Information criteria" in [Comparing candidate models](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-comparison).
6. Simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples from the model that the criteria prefer, calculate
   the scaled quantile residuals with DHARMa, and plot them, also against the concentration
   of the substrate. What do you see, and what can you conclude from 23 observations? Hint:
   proceed as in question 4 of Exercise 1 (the rates must be marked with `OBS()` in the
   NLL); the expected rate of an observation is the curve of its state at its
   concentration.

## Solution

### Question 1

Let $Y_i$ be the rate of the reaction in observation $i$ and $x_i$ the concentration of the
substrate. With one curve for both states, the model is

$$
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(f(x_i),\,\sigma^2\right),
\qquad
f(x)=\frac{ax}{b+x},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,23,
$$

where $a$ is the asymptote, the maximum rate of the reaction (counts/min/min), $b$ is the
half-maximum, the concentration at which the rate is $a/2$ (ppm), and $\sigma$ is the
standard deviation of the rates around the curve (counts/min/min). The mean of a Normal
distribution can take any value, and the curve is positive anyway for positive $a$ and
$b$. All three parameters are positive, so we optimise their logarithms.

The list of data holds the concentration, the rate and the number of the state of each
observation, which question 2 needs. `as.numeric()` of a factor returns the position of
each level, so 1 is a treated cell and 2 an untreated cell. Question 6 checks the model
that the criteria prefer, which we do not know yet, so we mark the rates with `OBS()` in
both NLLs:

```{r}
# Load the data and put the concentration (ppm), the rate (counts/min/min) and the number
# of the state of each observation (1 treated, 2 untreated) in a list of data.
data(Puromycin, package = "datasets")
levels(Puromycin$state)
enzyme_data = list(
  conc = Puromycin$conc,
  rate = Puromycin$rate,
  state = as.numeric(Puromycin$state)
)

# Negative log-likelihood of one Michaelis–Menten curve for both states.
pooled_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  rate = OBS(rate)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  mu = a * conc / (b + conc)
  -sum(dnorm(x = rate, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}
```

As starting values we take an asymptote of 190 counts/min/min, between the two values read
by eye, the half-maximum of 0.06 ppm read by eye and a standard deviation of 10
counts/min/min:

```{r}
# Starting values, process the NLL and fit it.
pooled_start = list(log_a = log(190), log_b = log(0.06), log_sigma = log(10))
pooled_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(pooled_nll, enzyme_data), pooled_start, silent = TRUE)
pooled_fit = optim(
  par = pooled_obj$par,
  fn = pooled_obj$fn,
  gr = pooled_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
pooled_fit$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale: a and sigma in counts/min/min, b in ppm.
c(a = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_b"]]),
  sigma = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_sigma"]]))
```

The fit converged, with $\hat a\approx191$ counts/min/min, $\hat b\approx0.060$ ppm and
$\hat\sigma\approx17.8$ counts/min/min. We draw the curve over the data
(@fig-puromycin_pooled):

```{r}
#| label: fig-puromycin_pooled
#| fig-cap: "Rate of an enzymatic reaction against the concentration of the substrate in cells treated with puromycin (filled circles) and in untreated cells (open circles), with one Michaelis–Menten curve for both states fitted by maximum likelihood."
# Michaelis–Menten function: asymptote a and half-maximum b.
michaelis_menten = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x / (b + x)
}

# Observations, with a filled symbol for the treated cells, and the fitted curve.
plot(rate ~ conc, data = Puromycin,
     pch = ifelse(Puromycin$state == "treated", 16, 1),
     xlab = "Concentration of substrate (ppm)", ylab = "Rate (counts/min/min)")
curve(michaelis_menten(x, a = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_a"]]),
                       b = exp(pooled_fit$par[["log_b"]])),
      add = TRUE, col = "#D55E00")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("treated", "untreated"), pch = c(16, 1), bty = "n")
```

The curve passes between the two groups: above 0.1 ppm, most treated cells lie above it and
most untreated cells below it.

### Question 2

In the second model the parameter `log_a` is a vector with the logarithms of the two
asymptotes, and `a[state]` selects the asymptote of the state of each observation. The NLL
also asks for the difference between the two asymptotes with `ADREPORT()`, which we use in
question 3. We start from the two asymptotes read by eye:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood with one asymptote for each state and a common b and sigma.
state_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  rate = OBS(rate)
  a = exp(log_a)
  b = exp(log_b)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma)
  # Difference between the asymptotes of the treated and the untreated cells.
  difference = a[1] - a[2]
  ADREPORT(difference)
  # a[state] is the asymptote of the state of each observation.
  mu = a[state] * conc / (b + conc)
  -sum(dnorm(x = rate, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

# Starting values: the asymptotes read by eye (treated, untreated), b and sigma as before.
state_start = list(log_a = log(c(210, 165)), log_b = log(0.06), log_sigma = log(10))
state_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(state_nll, enzyme_data), state_start, silent = TRUE)
state_fit = optim(
  par = state_obj$par,
  fn = state_obj$fn,
  gr = state_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
state_fit$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale. The first two elements of par are the two values of
# log_a (treated, untreated); unname() drops their names.
a_state = unname(exp(state_fit$par[1:2]))
b_state = exp(state_fit$par[["log_b"]])
sigma_state = exp(state_fit$par[["log_sigma"]])
c(a_treated = a_state[1], a_untreated = a_state[2], b = b_state, sigma = sigma_state)
```

The fit converged. The asymptote is about 209 counts/min/min for the treated cells and 167
for the untreated cells, the half-maximum is 0.058 ppm, and $\hat\sigma$ has fallen from
17.8 to 9.9 counts/min/min (@fig-puromycin_state). With one curve for both states, the
difference between the states is part of the spread of the rates around the curve. With
one asymptote for each state the curves describe that difference, and the spread that
remains is about half as large.

```{r}
#| label: fig-puromycin_state
#| fig-cap: "The same observations with a Michaelis–Menten curve for each state, with separate asymptotes and a common half-maximum, fitted by maximum likelihood: treated cells (filled circles, solid line) and untreated cells (open circles, dashed line)."
# Observations and one fitted curve for each state.
plot(rate ~ conc, data = Puromycin,
     pch = ifelse(Puromycin$state == "treated", 16, 1),
     xlab = "Concentration of substrate (ppm)", ylab = "Rate (counts/min/min)")
curve(michaelis_menten(x, a = a_state[1], b = b_state), add = TRUE, lty = 1, col = "#D55E00")
curve(michaelis_menten(x, a = a_state[2], b = b_state), add = TRUE, lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("treated", "untreated"),
       pch = c(16, 1), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

### Question 3

The row `difference` of the summary of `sdreport()` holds the estimate and the standard
error of the difference. A difference between two asymptotes can be positive or negative
and has no bound, so we calculate the Wald interval on the original scale, as for the
difference between two probabilities in the Chapter 4 practical:

```{r}
# Standard errors, and the 95% Wald interval of the difference between the asymptotes.
state_sd = sdreport(state_obj)
state_summary = summary(state_sd)
state_summary
state_summary["difference", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * state_summary["difference", "Std. Error"]
```

The asymptote of the treated cells is higher by 42 counts/min/min, with a 95% Wald
interval from 31 to 54 counts/min/min. So in this model the treatment with puromycin raises
the maximum rate of the reaction by about a quarter ($208.6/166.6\approx1.25$), while the
concentration at which the reaction reaches half of its maximum rate is the same in both
states. That the half-maximum is shared is an assumption of the model; a model with one
$b$ for each state could be fitted and compared with it in the same way as in question 5.

### Question 4

We profile $\log(b)$ and transform the endpoints back with `exp()`, and we calculate the
Wald interval from the row `log_b`, on the log scale, with its endpoints transformed back:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profile of log(b) and its 95% interval, transformed back (ppm). confint() warns about
# repeated values, as in Exercise 1.
state_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(state_obj, name = "log_b", trace = FALSE)
exp(confint(state_profile_b))

# Wald interval of b (ppm): calculated on the log scale, endpoints transformed back.
exp(state_summary["log_b", "Estimate"] +
      c(-1, 1) * critical_value * state_summary["log_b", "Std. Error"])
```

The likelihood profile interval goes from 0.047 to 0.071 ppm and the Wald interval from
0.048 to 0.071 ppm: their endpoints differ by less than 0.001 ppm. The difference from the reed
frogs is in the design. The concentrations of the experiment go from 0.02 to 1.1 ppm, about
19 times the half-maximum, so the observations cover the rise of the curve and also the
part where it levels off. Both parameters are then well determined, and the log-likelihood
is close to a parabola on the log scale, which is the approximation behind the Wald
interval. In the reed frog experiment the densities stopped below the half-maximum, so the
tanks said little about the asymptote, and the profile of the handling time was strongly
asymmetric.

### Question 5

The first model has $K=3$ parameters and the second $K=4$, and both are fitted to the same
23 observations, so $n=23$ in AICc and BIC:

```{r}
# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with n = 23 observations.
n_enzyme = length(enzyme_data$rate)
k_enzyme = c(pooled = 3, state = 4)
nll_enzyme = c(pooled = pooled_fit$value, state = state_fit$value)
aic_enzyme = 2 * k_enzyme + 2 * nll_enzyme
aicc_enzyme = aic_enzyme + 2 * k_enzyme * (k_enzyme + 1) / (n_enzyme - k_enzyme - 1)
bic_enzyme = k_enzyme * log(n_enzyme) + 2 * nll_enzyme
rbind(aic = aic_enzyme, aicc = aicc_enzyme, bic = bic_enzyme)
```

Every criterion prefers the model with one asymptote for each state, by 25.1 units of AIC,
24.1 of AICc and 24.0 of BIC. The criteria agree, and by a wide margin: the extra parameter
improves the fit far more than any of the penalties. This agrees with the halving of
$\hat\sigma$ in question 2.

### Question 6

We simulate from the model with one asymptote for each state, as in Exercise 1 (the rates
were marked with `OBS()` in question 1). The expected rate of each observation is the curve
of its state at its concentration. `DHARMa::plotQQunif()` draws only the left panel of
`plot()`, the quantile–quantile plot; we use it because the residuals against the
concentration, which `DHARMa::plotResiduals()` draws, replace the right panel:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.5
# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 23 rates at the estimates.
state_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = n_enzyme, ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 621)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  state_simulations[, j] = state_obj$simulate(state_fit$par)$rate
}

# Expected rate of each observation, and the scaled quantile residuals.
state_expected = michaelis_menten(enzyme_data$conc, a = a_state[enzyme_data$state],
                                  b = b_state)
state_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = state_simulations,
  observedResponse = enzyme_data$rate,
  fittedPredictedResponse = state_expected,
  integerResponse = FALSE
)

# Quantile–quantile plot, and residuals against the concentration of the substrate.
DHARMa::plotQQunif(state_residuals)
DHARMa::plotResiduals(state_residuals, form = enzyme_data$conc)
```

The quantile–quantile plot follows the line, so the residuals as a whole are close to
uniform. Against the concentration they show a pattern: they tend to lie above 0.5 at the
lowest concentration and at the two highest, and below 0.5 at the intermediate
concentrations. That is, the observed rates lie above the curves at both ends and below
them in the middle, as if the rate bent towards its maximum more gradually than a
Michaelis–Menten curve can. However, there are only three or four observations at each
concentration, and a pattern of this size can arise by chance with 23 observations (DHARMa
draws one quartile in red, but its combined test does not flag the pattern), so the plot is
a hint and not a conclusion. A curve with a third parameter that changes how gradually the
curve bends could be fitted and compared with the criteria of question 5.

# Exercise 3: Fecundity of fir trees

The data set `FirDBHFec_sum` in the package `emdbook` contains the diameter at breast
height (`DBH`, in cm) and the fecundity (`fecundity`) of 333 balsam fir trees (*Abies
balsamea*) on Whiteface Mountain, New York (Silvertown and Dodd 1999; Dodd and Silvertown
2000). Fecundity was measured as the number of cone rachises on a tree: the rachis is the
axis of a cone, which stays on the branch after the cone has fallen apart. Load the data
with `data(FirDBHFec_sum, package = "emdbook")`.

In Exercise 7 of the Chapter 5 practical we described the mean fecundity with a
[power law](../../Supplements/deterministic-functions.qmd#sec-fn-power),
$\mu(x)=ax^b$, where $x$ is the diameter, and read $a=0.5$ and $b=2$ from two points of the
cloud. The trees come from two populations (the column `pop`). We do not model this
grouping: we treat the trees as independent observations of one curve, which is a
simplification ([Chapter 7](../../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) deals with observations that come
in groups).

1. As in Exercise 7 of the Chapter 5 practical, remove the trees with a missing diameter,
   and check that no fecundity is missing. Why can a missing value not be replaced by
   zero? Some fecundities are not whole numbers: find them and decide what to do with them
   before you fit a model for counts. Hint: `x != round(x)` is `TRUE` for the elements of
   `x` that are not whole numbers. Rounding them and removing those trees are both
   defensible; say which you choose and why.
2. Write a [Poisson](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-poisson) model whose mean
   follows the power law, with the units of $a$. Fit it from the values read by eye in
   the Chapter 5 practical, and check it with scaled quantile residuals from DHARMa and the
   dispersion statistic. Hint: the mean must be positive, but the exponent $b$ can take any
   real value, so only $a$ needs a transformation (see
   [From a response curve to a model for observations](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-observation)).
   For the residuals, follow
   [Checking the fitted model](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-residuals): the counts are whole
   numbers, as the numbers killed of the reed frogs were.
3. Fit a [Negative Binomial](../../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial)
   model with the same curve, with `dnbinom2()` of RTMBdist (mean and shape $k$). Check its
   residuals, and draw the curves of both models over the data. Hint: `dnbinom2()` takes
   the mean in `mu` and the shape, which is positive, in `size`.
4. Compare the two models with AIC, AICc and BIC. Hint: $n$ is the number of trees (see
   "Information criteria" in [Comparing candidate models](../Theory.qmd#sec-response-comparison)).
5. For the model that the criteria prefer, calculate the likelihood profile interval of the
   exponent $b$, and from it an interval for the factor $2^b$ by which the mean fecundity
   changes when the diameter doubles. Do the data support a fecundity proportional to the
   cross-sectional area of the trunk ($b=2$)? Hint: see "Likelihood profile intervals of
   the parameters" in [Uncertainty of a response curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-curve-uncertainty)
   for transforming the endpoints of an interval; $2^b$ increases with $b$.
6. For the same model, calculate the mean fecundity on a grid of diameters from 3 to 18 cm
   with `ADREPORT()`, and its pointwise 95% confidence band from Wald intervals on the log
   scale. Draw the curve and its band over the data. Where along the diameters is the
   curve best determined, and why? Hint: follow
   [Uncertainty of the fitted curve](../Theory.qmd#sec-delta-method), with the logarithm of
   the mean in place of the logit of the probability; `lines()` adds the curve and the two
   limits of the band to the plot.

## Solution

### Question 1

We count the missing values in each column with `is.na()`, keep the trees for which both
are known, and look for fecundities that are not whole numbers:

```{r}
# Load the fir data and count the missing diameters and fecundities.
data(FirDBHFec_sum, package = "emdbook")
nrow(FirDBHFec_sum)
colSums(is.na(FirDBHFec_sum[, c("DBH", "fecundity")]))

# Keep the trees with both a diameter and a fecundity.
complete = !is.na(FirDBHFec_sum$DBH) & !is.na(FirDBHFec_sum$fecundity)
fir = FirDBHFec_sum[complete, ]
nrow(fir)

# Fecundities that are not whole numbers.
fir$fecundity[fir$fecundity != round(fir$fecundity)]
```

The diameter is missing for 22 trees and the fecundity for none, so 311 trees remain. A
missing value means that the quantity was not recorded. Replacing it by zero would add
observations that were never made (a tree with a diameter of zero, or without any cones)
and would pull the curve towards them. Removing the incomplete rows assumes instead that
whether a value was recorded does not depend on the fecundity of the tree.

Six fecundities are not whole numbers, for example 206.5. The help page does not explain
them, but in the full data set `FirDBHFec` of the same package the yearly counts of these
six trees include fractions (such as 32.5 cones in one year). The Poisson and Negative
Binomial distributions describe whole numbers, so we round the six values to the nearest
whole number, which changes each of them by at most half a rachis (removing the six trees
would be the alternative, at the cost of six observations). The list of data holds
the diameter (cm) and the number of rachises:

```{r}
# Diameter (cm) and fecundity, rounded to whole numbers of rachises.
fir_data = list(dbh = fir$DBH, cones = round(fir$fecundity))
```

### Question 2

Let $Y_i$ be the number of rachises of tree $i$ and $x_i$ its diameter. The model is

$$
Y_i \sim \operatorname{Poisson}\left(\mu(x_i)\right),
\qquad
\mu(x)=a\,x^b,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,311.
$$

The mean of a Poisson distribution must be positive, and the power law is positive for any
$b$ when $a$ and $x$ are positive, so we optimise $\log(a)$ and leave the exponent $b$
untransformed: it can take any real value. The units of $a$ follow from the curve: $ax^b$
is a number of rachises and $x^b$ is in cm$^b$, so $a$ is in rachises/cm$^b$, units that
depend on the estimate of the exponent (rachises/cm² for $b=2$). This makes $a$ hard to
interpret on its own, and we will interpret $b$ and quantities calculated from it. We mark
the counts with `OBS()` for the residuals and start from the values read by eye:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the power law with a Poisson observation model.
poisson_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  cones = OBS(cones)
  a = exp(log_a)
  # Mean number of rachises of a tree of each diameter.
  mu = a * dbh^b
  -sum(dpois(x = cones, lambda = mu, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL from the values read by eye in the Chapter 5 practical, and fit it.
poisson_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(poisson_nll, fir_data),
  list(log_a = log(0.5), b = 2),
  silent = TRUE
)
poisson_fit = optim(
  par = poisson_obj$par,
  fn = poisson_obj$fn,
  gr = poisson_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
poisson_fit$convergence
c(a = exp(poisson_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = poisson_fit$par[["b"]])
```

The fit converged, with $\hat b\approx1.98$, close to the exponent of 2 read by eye. We
simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 311 trees and calculate the residuals. The
counts are whole numbers, so `integerResponse = TRUE`. The element `scaledResiduals` of the
result holds the residuals, and a residual of exactly 0 or 1 marks a tree whose count lies
outside the range of all its simulated values, so we also count those trees:

```{r}
#| label: fig-fir_poisson_residuals
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Poisson model with a power law for the fecundity of 311 fir trees, from 1,000 hypothetical samples. Stars mark trees whose counts lie outside the range of their simulated values."
# Power law: a is the value at x = 1 and b is the exponent.
power_law = function(x, a = 1, b = 1) {
  a * x^b
}

# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 311 trees at the estimates.
n_trees = length(fir_data$cones)
poisson_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = n_trees, ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 631)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  poisson_simulations[, j] = poisson_obj$simulate(poisson_fit$par)$cones
}

# Scaled quantile residuals and the two standard panels.
poisson_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = poisson_simulations,
  observedResponse = fir_data$cones,
  fittedPredictedResponse = power_law(fir_data$dbh, a = exp(poisson_fit$par[["log_a"]]),
                                      b = poisson_fit$par[["b"]]),
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
plot(poisson_residuals)

# Trees outside the range of their simulations, and the dispersion statistic.
sum(poisson_residuals$scaledResiduals %in% c(0, 1))
DHARMa::testDispersion(poisson_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
```

The Poisson model does not describe these data. The residuals are far from uniform: most of
them are close to 0 or 1, and 147 of the 311 trees have counts outside the range of all
their 1,000 simulated values. The dispersion statistic is about 23, so the counts vary
around the curve about 23 times as much (as a variance) as the Poisson distribution allows.
Trees of the same diameter differ in fecundity for many reasons that the curve does not
contain, and the Poisson model, whose variance equals its mean, leaves no room for them.

### Question 3

The Negative Binomial model keeps the curve for the mean and adds the shape $k$, which is
positive, so we optimise $\log(k)$. `dnbinom2()` of RTMBdist takes the mean in `mu` and the
shape in `size`. We start from the values by eye and a shape of 1:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the power law with a Negative Binomial observation model.
nbinom_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  cones = OBS(cones)
  a = exp(log_a)
  k = exp(log_k)
  mu = a * dbh^b
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = cones, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the NLL from the values read by eye and a shape of 1, and fit it.
nbinom_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nbinom_nll, fir_data),
  list(log_a = log(0.5), b = 2, log_k = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
nbinom_fit = optim(
  par = nbinom_obj$par,
  fn = nbinom_obj$fn,
  gr = nbinom_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
nbinom_fit$convergence
c(a = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = nbinom_fit$par[["b"]],
  k = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_k"]]))
```

The fit converged, with $\hat b\approx1.80$ and $\hat k\approx1.84$. We check the
residuals as for the Poisson model:

```{r}
#| label: fig-fir_nbinom_residuals
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the Negative Binomial model with a power law for the fecundity of 311 fir trees, from 1,000 hypothetical samples."
# 1,000 hypothetical samples of the 311 trees at the estimates.
nbinom_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = n_trees, ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 632)
for (j in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  nbinom_simulations[, j] = nbinom_obj$simulate(nbinom_fit$par)$cones
}

# Scaled quantile residuals, the two standard panels and the dispersion statistic.
nbinom_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = nbinom_simulations,
  observedResponse = fir_data$cones,
  fittedPredictedResponse = power_law(fir_data$dbh, a = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_a"]]),
                                      b = nbinom_fit$par[["b"]]),
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
plot(nbinom_residuals)
DHARMa::testDispersion(nbinom_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
```

The Negative Binomial model describes the variation among trees far better. The
quantile–quantile plot follows the line, and only one tree (the star) lies outside the
range of its simulations. A smaller disagreement remains. The dispersion statistic is below
one, so the counts vary around the curve somewhat less than the model allows, and in the
right panel the lower quartile of the residuals rises from below 0.25 for the trees with
the smallest expected fecundity to above 0.25 for the largest: large trees seldom have the
very low counts that the model expects for some of them. Under a Negative Binomial model
with one shape the variance, $\mu+\mu^2/k$, grows with the square of the mean, and the
residuals suggest that the variation among the largest trees grows less than that. A possible
revision would let the shape depend on the diameter. For the questions of this exercise,
which concern the curve, the remaining disagreement is small compared with that of the
Poisson model.

Both curves are drawn over the data in @fig-fir_curves:

```{r}
#| label: fig-fir_curves
#| fig-cap: "Fecundity of 311 balsam fir trees against their diameter at breast height, with the power law fitted by maximum likelihood under a Negative Binomial model (solid line) and under a Poisson model (dashed line)."
# Observations and the two fitted curves.
plot(fecundity ~ DBH, data = fir,
     xlab = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", ylab = "Fecundity (cone rachises)")
curve(power_law(x, a = exp(nbinom_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = nbinom_fit$par[["b"]]),
      add = TRUE, lty = 1, col = "#D55E00")
curve(power_law(x, a = exp(poisson_fit$par[["log_a"]]), b = poisson_fit$par[["b"]]),
      add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Negative Binomial", "Poisson"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("#D55E00", "black"), bty = "n")
```

The two curves are almost the same for trees up to about 10 cm, and above that the
Negative Binomial curve lies below the Poisson curve. The two models weight the trees
differently. Under the
Negative Binomial model the variance grows with the square of the mean, so the large counts
of the largest trees are less informative about the curve than under the Poisson model,
whose variance grows only in proportion to the mean.

### Question 4

The Poisson model has $K=2$ parameters and the Negative Binomial model $K=3$, and $n$ is the
number of trees, 311:

```{r}
# AIC, AICc and BIC of the two models, with n = 311 trees.
k_fir = c(poisson = 2, nbinom = 3)
nll_fir = c(poisson = poisson_fit$value, nbinom = nbinom_fit$value)
aic_fir = 2 * k_fir + 2 * nll_fir
aicc_fir = aic_fir + 2 * k_fir * (k_fir + 1) / (n_trees - k_fir - 1)
bic_fir = k_fir * log(n_trees) + 2 * nll_fir
rbind(aic = aic_fir, aicc = aicc_fir, bic = bic_fir)
```

All three criteria prefer the Negative Binomial model by about 5,000 units. With 311 trees
the correction of AICc is negligible, and the extra cost of the shape in BIC ($\log(311)$
instead of 2) is tiny compared with the difference in log-likelihood. The comparison agrees
with the residuals of questions 2 and 3.

### Question 5

The exponent is not transformed in the NLL, so `confint()` of its profile gives the
interval of $b$ directly. The function $2^b$ increases with $b$, so the endpoints of the
interval of $b$ give an interval for $2^b$ in the same order:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Profile of b and its 95% interval (confint() warns about repeated values, as before).
nbinom_profile_b = TMB::tmbprofile(nbinom_obj, name = "b", trace = FALSE)
b_interval_fir = confint(nbinom_profile_b)
b_interval_fir

# 95% interval for the factor 2^b, from the endpoints of the interval of b.
2^b_interval_fir
```

The exponent is estimated at 1.80, with a likelihood profile interval from 1.55 to 2.05.
When the diameter doubles, the mean fecundity is multiplied by $2^{1.80}\approx3.5$, with
an interval from 2.9 to 4.2.

The value $b=2$, for which the fecundity would be proportional to the cross-sectional area
of the trunk, lies inside the interval of $b$, close to its upper end. So the data do not
rule out this proportionality, but they favour a smaller exponent, for which the mean
fecundity increases by a factor of about 3.5 and not 4 when the diameter doubles. Note that
the Poisson model, with $\hat b\approx1.98$, would have suggested an exponent of 2 with an
interval that is much too narrow, because it treats the trees as far less variable than
they are.

### Question 6

As in the theory, we add a grid of diameters to the list of data, as `dbh_grid`, and
calculate the curve on the grid inside the NLL. The mean fecundity is positive, so we ask
for its logarithm with `ADREPORT()`, a scale on which it is unbounded. We process the new
NLL, fit it again (the estimates do not change) and call `sdreport()`:

```{r}
# A grid of diameters (cm), added to the list of data.
dbh_grid = seq(from = 3, to = 18, by = 0.1)
fir_data$dbh_grid = dbh_grid

# The Negative Binomial NLL with three more lines.
nbinom_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  cones = OBS(cones)
  a = exp(log_a)
  k = exp(log_k)
  mu = a * dbh^b
  # The logarithm of the mean fecundity at every diameter of the grid.
  mu_grid = a * dbh_grid^b
  log_mu_grid = log(mu_grid)
  ADREPORT(log_mu_grid)
  -sum(dnbinom2(x = cones, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# Process the new NLL, fit it again and calculate the standard errors.
nbinom_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(nbinom_nll, fir_data),
  list(log_a = log(0.5), b = 2, log_k = log(1)),
  silent = TRUE
)
nbinom_fit = optim(
  par = nbinom_obj$par,
  fn = nbinom_obj$fn,
  gr = nbinom_obj$gr,
  method = "BFGS"
)
nbinom_fit$convergence
nbinom_sd = sdreport(nbinom_obj)
```

With `select = "report"`, `summary()` returns one row per diameter of the grid. We
calculate the Wald interval of each row on the log scale, and transform the curve and the
endpoints back with `exp()` to draw them over the data (@fig-fir_band):

```{r}
#| label: fig-fir_band
#| fig-cap: "Fecundity of 311 balsam fir trees against their diameter at breast height, with the power law fitted by maximum likelihood under a Negative Binomial model (solid line) and its pointwise 95% confidence band (dashed lines), calculated from Wald intervals on the log scale."
# Rows of log_mu_grid: one per diameter of the grid.
band_summary = summary(nbinom_sd, select = "report")

# Wald intervals on the log scale.
log_lower = band_summary[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]
log_upper = band_summary[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * band_summary[, "Std. Error"]

# Observations, and the curve and its band transformed back to numbers of rachises.
plot(fecundity ~ DBH, data = fir,
     xlab = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", ylab = "Fecundity (cone rachises)")
lines(dbh_grid, exp(band_summary[, "Estimate"]), col = "#D55E00")
lines(dbh_grid, exp(log_lower), lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")
lines(dbh_grid, exp(log_upper), lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Fitted curve", "95% confidence band"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = "#D55E00", bty = "n")
```

The band is pointwise: at each diameter, the interval contains the mean fecundity of the
data generating process at that diameter in approximately 95% of hypothetical samples. On
the log scale it is narrowest at about 8 cm, where the standard error of the logarithm of
the mean is 0.043, so the interval extends about 8% on either side of the curve. It widens
towards both ends, to standard errors of 0.13 at 3 cm and 0.11 at 17.4 cm, the largest
tree. On the log scale the curve is a straight line in $\log(x)$,
$\log(\mu(x))=\log(a)+b\log(x)$, and a line fitted to data is best determined in the
middle of the observations, here around the geometric mean of the diameters, 7.9 cm. Half
of the trees have diameters between 6.5 and 9.8 cm, and only six are larger than 15 cm, so
away from the middle a change in the exponent moves the curve more and fewer trees hold it
in place. On the original scale the band also widens because it is multiplied by the
mean: at 8 cm it runs from about 39 to 46 rachises, and at 17.4 cm from about 138 to 212.
The band describes the uncertainty of the mean fecundity; the fecundities of single trees
vary much more around the curve, as the cloud of points shows.

# Exercise 4: Coverage of an interval for the time of the peak

This exercise is extra practice. In Exercise 1 the Wald interval and the likelihood profile
interval for the time of the peak differed, and from one sample we cannot tell how often
either of them contains the time of the peak of the data generating process. As in
Exercise 5 of the [Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd), we
can find out by simulating hypothetical samples from a model whose parameters we know:
here the Normal model fitted in Exercise 1, with the estimates as its parameters (see
"Coverage checked by simulation" in
[Chapter 4](../../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty)). This exercise
continues with the objects of Exercise 1. The function that runs the simulation is given
below the questions with two gaps, which you fill in.

1. Complete the first gap of the function `simulate_peak_time()` below. Set seed 641 and
   simulate 2,000 hypothetical samples of the 27 titres, on the same days, from the fitted
   Normal model. Each sample is fitted from the values read by eye, as the data were. How
   many fits failed? Calculate the bias of the estimator of the time of the peak, with its
   Monte Carlo standard error, and compare the standard deviation of the estimates with
   the standard error of Exercise 1. Hint: the list of data of each sample needs the names
   that `normal_nll()` uses, `day` and `titre`. The bias is the mean of the estimates minus
   the time of the peak used to simulate, $1/\hat b$ of Exercise 1. A **Monte Carlo standard
   error** measures how much a result of the simulation would vary if it were repeated with
   other random samples; for the bias, a mean of 2,000 estimates, it is the standard
   deviation of the estimates divided by $\sqrt{2000}$.
2. Complete the second gap, which calculates the 95% Wald interval for the time of the
   peak from the row of `ADREPORT()`, and calculate the coverage of the interval with its
   Monte Carlo standard error. (The coverage of the likelihood profile interval would need
   `tmbprofile()` in every sample, which takes much longer, so we do not simulate it
   here.) Hint: the coverage is a proportion $c$ of 2,000 samples, so its Monte Carlo
   standard error is $\sqrt{c(1-c)/2000}$, as in the solution of Exercise 5 of the
   [Chapter 4 practical](../../Chapter_4/Practicals/solution.qmd).
3. In how many samples does the interval lie entirely below the time of the peak that was
   used to simulate, and in how many entirely above it? What does this suggest, given the
   two intervals of question 3 of Exercise 1?
4. Why do these results only approximate the behaviour of the interval for the real
   rabbits?

The function below needs `normal_nll()`, `normal_obj`, `normal_fit`, `titre_data` and
`titre_start` from Exercise 1, the helper `cmb()`, and the object `critical_value` (the
critical value of the standard Normal distribution for a 95% interval). It draws every
sample with the function `simulate()` of the fitted object, and stores the results of
every sample in one row of a data frame. In each gap, replace `NA` by your own code. The
lines that follow a gap use the names of the objects that the gap creates, so keep those
names.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Hypothetical samples of the 27 titres from the Normal model fitted in Exercise 1. For
# each sample: the estimate of the time of the peak, its 95% Wald interval, and whether
# the fit converged.
simulate_peak_time = function(n_samples) {
  results = data.frame(
    estimate = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    lower = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    upper = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    converged = rep(NA, times = n_samples)
  )
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample: titres on the same days, simulated at the estimates.
    titre_sim = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre

    # GAP 1: connect normal_nll() to the days and the simulated titres and process it
    # with MakeADFun(), starting from titre_start, and store the result in an object
    # called sim_obj. Then fit it with optim() and method = "BFGS", and store the result
    # in an object called sim_fit.
    sim_obj = NA
    sim_fit = NA

    # GAP 2: from the row peak_time of summary(sdreport(sim_obj), select = "report"),
    # the estimate of the time of the peak and the endpoints of its 95% Wald interval on
    # the original scale, in objects called estimate, lower and upper.
    estimate = NA
    lower = NA
    upper = NA

    results$estimate[i] = estimate
    results$lower[i] = lower
    results$upper[i] = upper
    results$converged[i] = sim_fit$convergence == 0
  }
  results
}
```

## Solution

### Question 1

Here is the function with its two gaps filled in. For each sample, gap 1 fits the model to
the simulated titres exactly as Exercise 1 fitted it to the data, with `cmb()`,
`MakeADFun()` and `optim()` from the values read by eye. Gap 2 takes the estimate and the
standard error of the time of the peak from the row of `ADREPORT()` and calculates the Wald
interval on the original scale, as in question 3 of Exercise 1:

```{r}
# Hypothetical samples of the 27 titres from the Normal model fitted in Exercise 1. For
# each sample: the estimate of the time of the peak, its 95% Wald interval, and whether
# the fit converged.
simulate_peak_time = function(n_samples) {
  results = data.frame(
    estimate = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    lower = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    upper = rep(NA, times = n_samples),
    converged = rep(NA, times = n_samples)
  )
  for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
    # One hypothetical sample: titres on the same days, simulated at the estimates.
    titre_sim = normal_obj$simulate(normal_fit$par)$titre

    # Gap 1: fit the model to the simulated titres from the values read by eye.
    sim_obj = MakeADFun(
      cmb(normal_nll, list(day = titre_data$day, titre = titre_sim)),
      titre_start,
      silent = TRUE
    )
    sim_fit = optim(par = sim_obj$par, fn = sim_obj$fn, gr = sim_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

    # Gap 2: estimate and 95% Wald interval of the time of the peak, on the original scale.
    sim_report = summary(sdreport(sim_obj), select = "report")
    estimate = sim_report["peak_time", "Estimate"]
    lower = estimate - critical_value * sim_report["peak_time", "Std. Error"]
    upper = estimate + critical_value * sim_report["peak_time", "Std. Error"]

    results$estimate[i] = estimate
    results$lower[i] = lower
    results$upper[i] = upper
    results$converged[i] = sim_fit$convergence == 0
  }
  results
}
```

The time of the peak that the samples are simulated from is $1/\hat b$ of Exercise 1. We
run the simulation (about half a minute) and count the failed fits, both those with a
convergence code other than zero and those for which `sdreport()` could not calculate a
standard error:

```{r}
# 2,000 hypothetical samples from the model fitted in Exercise 1.
set.seed(seed = 641)
n_samples = 2000
peak_samples = simulate_peak_time(n_samples)

# Time of the peak used to simulate (days), and the number of failed fits.
peak_time_sim = 1 / b_mle
peak_time_sim
sum(!peak_samples$converged | is.na(peak_samples$lower))
```

No fit failed. Had some failed, we would report how many and count them in the coverage
(for example as intervals that miss), because leaving them out silently would hide the
samples in which the method breaks down. The bias is the mean of the estimates minus the
time of the peak used to simulate. Its Monte Carlo standard error, the standard error of a
mean of 2,000 values, is the standard deviation of the estimates divided by
$\sqrt{2000}$:

```{r}
# Bias of the estimator of the time of the peak, its Monte Carlo standard error, and the
# standard deviation of the estimates next to the standard error of Exercise 1.
c(
  bias = mean(peak_samples$estimate) - peak_time_sim,
  mc_se_bias = sd(peak_samples$estimate) / sqrt(n_samples),
  sd_estimates = sd(peak_samples$estimate),
  se_exercise_1 = summary(normal_sd, select = "report")["peak_time", "Std. Error"]
)
```

The bias is 0.019 days, about two Monte Carlo standard errors (0.0085 days) from zero. So
the estimator may be slightly biased upwards, but by about 0.3% of the time of the peak,
which is negligible compared with its standard error. The standard deviation of the
estimates across the hypothetical samples, 0.381 days, agrees with the standard error that
`sdreport()` calculated from the curvature of the log-likelihood of the data, 0.383 days.
With 27 observations the standard error describes the spread of the estimator well.

### Question 2

The interval contains the time of the peak used to simulate when its lower endpoint is
below that value and its upper endpoint above it. The coverage is the fraction of samples
in which this is the case, and its Monte Carlo standard error is that of a proportion:

```{r}
# Coverage of the Wald interval, and its Monte Carlo standard error.
covered = peak_samples$lower <= peak_time_sim & peak_time_sim <= peak_samples$upper
coverage = mean(covered)
c(coverage = coverage, mc_se = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_samples))
```

The coverage is 0.927, with a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.006, so it lies about four
standard errors below the nominal 0.95. The Wald interval of the time of the peak contains
the value used to simulate slightly less often than its confidence level states: with 27
observations it is an approximation.

### Question 3

An interval lies entirely below the value used to simulate when its upper endpoint is
below that value, and entirely above it when its lower endpoint is above it:

```{r}
# Intervals that miss on each side of the time of the peak used to simulate.
c(
  below = sum(peak_samples$upper < peak_time_sim),
  above = sum(peak_samples$lower > peak_time_sim)
)
```

Of the 147 intervals that miss, 104 lie below the time of the peak used to simulate and 43
above it. A good interval would miss about equally often on both sides (about 50 times on
each side in 2,000 samples). The Wald interval is symmetric around the estimate, whereas
in question 3 of Exercise 1 the likelihood profile interval extended further above the
estimate than below it, which is what an interval needs in order to miss less often on the
low side. This suggests that the profile interval would have a coverage closer to 95% and
that it would miss more evenly on both sides. Only a simulation that calculates the profile
interval in every sample could show this.

### Question 4

The simulation describes the behaviour of the interval when the data generating process is
the fitted model: titres that follow a Ricker curve exactly, with the estimates of Exercise
1 as its parameters, and that vary around it according to a Normal distribution with the
same standard deviation on every day, independently of each other. The parameters of the
process that generated the real titres are unknown and differ from the estimates, and the
coverage would be somewhat different with other parameter values. The model is also an
approximation: the residuals of Exercise 1 suggested that the titre levels off after its
peak, which a Ricker curve cannot do, and the titres of the real rabbits need not be
independent or Normal. With a misspecified model the properties of estimators and
intervals change (see [Misspecified models](../../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-misspecified)),
which this simulation does not explore. So the results approximate the behaviour of the
interval for the real rabbits, and the approximation is better the closer the fitted model
is to the data generating process.
